paragraphs.source_en: “The one at Konodai is the Bell-Hanging Pine; the one here at Dote Sanbancho is the Neck-Hanging Pine. Why did it get such a name? Well, from old times there has been a tradition that whoever comes under this pine tree feels like hanging himself. There are dozens of pines along the embankment, but whenever someone is found to have hanged himself, and people rush over to look, he is always hanging from this tree. Every year two or three people are sure to hang themselves there; somehow none of them can bring themselves to die on any other pine. When I looked, one horizontal branch of that pine stretched out conveniently over the road. The shape of the branch was truly elegant, and I thought it would be a terrible waste to leave it unused; best of all would be to have someone hanging there. I looked all around, wondering whether anyone might come, but unfortunately there was not a soul in sight. There was nothing for it, and at the time I wondered whether I should hang there myself. No, no; if I were to hang there myself, I would lose my life. It was too dangerous, so I had better give it up. But I had heard that the ancient Greeks, at banquets, used to add to the entertainment by pretending to hang themselves: one man would climb onto a platform, and just as he put his neck into the noose, another would kick the platform away; at the very moment the platform was pulled out, the man in the noose would loosen the knot and jump down. If that was really so, there was no particular need to be afraid. I thought I would try it too, and when I put my hand on the branch, it bent in just the right way; the manner of its bending was truly beautiful. When I imagined a neck caught on it, lightly bobbing up and down, I was beside myself with delight. I was determined to give it a try, but then I thought that if Tofu came and was waiting for me at home, it would be rather inconsiderate. So I changed my mind: first I would go meet Tofu and have our promised talk, and then I would come back. And so I went home.”

paragraphs.source_en: “That day there was a year-end party combined with an ensemble concert at a friend’s house in Mukojima, and I took a violin along with me. Fifteen or sixteen young ladies and wives had gathered, and it was quite a lively affair. Everything had been arranged perfectly; one might say it was one of the rare pleasures of recent days. Dinner was over, the ensemble playing was finished, conversation had begun on every side, and as it had grown rather late I was thinking of taking my leave of the host. Just then, the wife of a certain doctor came to my side and asked in a low voice, ‘Did you know that Miss So-and-so is ill?’ As it happened, when I had seen the young lady two or three days before, she was just as usual and showed no sign of being unwell anywhere, so I was startled and asked carefully about her condition. I was told that on the very night I had seen her, she suddenly developed a fever and began constantly uttering all sorts of delirious words. If that had been all, it would have been one thing, but in those delirious utterances my name kept appearing from time to time.”

paragraphs.source_zh: “那天在向岛的一个朋友家里开‘忘年会’兼合奏会，我也带了一把小提琴去。到了十五六位小姐和太太，是个非常热闹的盛会。一切都已准备停当，可以说这是最近难得的一次快举。晚餐已毕，乐器合奏也完了，大家进入闲谈，时间已经相当晚，我想向主人告辞。就在这时，某博士的夫人来到我的身旁，小声问我说：‘您知道某某小姐生病了吗？’说来，我两三天前见到那位小姐的时候，她还和平常一样，看不出她哪个地方不舒服，所以我吃了一惊，仔细问了情况。据说在我见到她的那天晚上，她突然发烧，不断发出谵语。如果只是这样，也就罢了，可她那谵语中，不时出现我的名字。”
